title: Gulliver’s Travels
author: Jonathan Swift
setting: Four voyages out of Bristol and Wapping between 1699 and 1715, to countries placed just off the edge of the real charts
lengthNote: Four parts of eight to twelve chapters each, around 105,000 words, with prefatory documents by a publisher and by Gulliver himself
openingLine: My father had a small estate in Nottinghamshire: I was the third of five sons.
summary: A ship’s surgeon writes up four voyages in the flat, dated, measured prose of factual travel literature, and each one leaves him a worse judge of his own species than the last. He is a giant, then a pet, then a tourist among projectors and immortals, and finally a man who cannot bear the smell of his wife. Swift’s method is to keep the reporting exact and let the reader supply the judgement that Gulliver withholds.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Gulliver’s Travels
sourceText.note: A proofed transcription of the text as corrected for Faulkner’s Dublin edition. References give the part and the chapter, which are the divisions the book itself uses; the prefatory letter to Sympson stands outside them.

structure.label: Prefatory documents
structure.title: The publisher’s note and Gulliver’s letter
structure.summary: Before the first voyage the reader is given a publisher’s note vouching for Gulliver’s character and a furious letter from Gulliver complaining that his cousin Sympson pressed him into publishing and then let the text be tampered with. The satire is under way before the travels begin: the apparatus that guarantees a true account is the first thing shown to be unreliable.

scenes.title: Richard Sympson’s note
scenes.summary: A cousin certifies Gulliver’s plain style, his reputation for truth in Redriff, and the cuts he has made to the manuscript.

scenes.ref: A Letter from Captain Gulliver to His Cousin Sympson
scenes.title: The author’s disavowal
scenes.summary: Gulliver complains of interpolations, of the failure of his book to reform anybody in six months, and of the sea Yahoos who fault his sea-language.

structure.label: Part I
structure.title: Lilliput
structure.summary: Shipwrecked and pegged to the ground by people a twelfth his size, Gulliver is fed, inventoried, made a Nardac and used as a naval weapon. Court office is won by rope-dancing, national identity rests on which end of an egg is broken, and the reward for putting out a palace fire is a charge of high treason. He leaves before his eyes can be put out.

scenes.title: Bound, fed and searched
scenes.summary: The shore, the cords, the first meal, and an official inventory of his pockets in which a watch is filed as a possible god.

scenes.title: Rope-dancers and egg-breakers
scenes.summary: Preferment by acrobatics; Reldresal explains the Tramecksan and Slamecksan, and the war with Blefuscu over the larger end of an egg.

scenes.title: A fleet, and a fire
scenes.summary: Gulliver hauls away the enemy navy, refuses to help enslave Blefuscu, and extinguishes a fire in the empress’s apartment in the most efficient available way.

scenes.title: Articles of impeachment
scenes.summary: A friend reads him the charges and the merciful sentence of blinding; he walks to Blefuscu and sails home in a real boat.

structure.label: Part II
structure.title: Brobdingnag
structure.summary: Left on a beach where the corn is forty feet high, Gulliver becomes a farm curiosity, then a queen’s pet, then a lecturer on England to a king. Everything he is proud of in England (the constitution, the law, finance, gunpowder) is laid before a listener who neither flatters him nor interrupts, and who is appalled when he has finished.

scenes.title: Found in the corn
scenes.summary: A giant reaper picks him up; the farmer exhibits him in market towns until he is nearly worked to death, cared for by the daughter he calls Glumdalclitch.

scenes.title: Bought by the queen
scenes.summary: The court scholars classify him as a freak of nature, and he begins to see European faces as skin and pores.

scenes.title: Indignities
scenes.summary: Wasps, apples, a monkey, a dwarf and the maids of honour: the body is the subject of the middle chapters.

scenes.title: Gunpowder refused
scenes.summary: Gulliver offers the recipe for artillery as a gift and is refused with horror; an eagle carries his box out to sea and he is picked up by an English ship.

structure.label: Part III
structure.title: Laputa, Balnibarbi and the Struldbrugs
structure.summary: The loosest and most various of the voyages: a flying island whose philosophers must be struck with bladders to attend to anything, a ruined country improved into famine by its academy, a governor who can raise the dead, and the Struldbrugs, who are immortal but not young. The target throughout is reason cut off from ordinary life.

scenes.title: The flying island
scenes.summary: Pirates, then Laputa: music, mathematics, terror of comets, and a king who suppresses rebellion by lowering the island onto the town.

scenes.title: The Academy of Lagado
scenes.summary: Munodi’s prosperous estate is a scandal to his neighbours; the projectors extract sunbeams from cucumbers and build houses from the roof down.

scenes.title: Glubbdubdrib
scenes.summary: The dead are summoned and modern history is corrected; the honours of the last century turn out to have been bought.

scenes.title: Luggnagg and the Struldbrugs
scenes.summary: Gulliver plans a glorious immortal life, then meets people who have had one for two hundred years.

structure.label: Part IV
structure.title: The land of the Houyhnhnms
structure.summary: Set ashore by his own mutinous crew, Gulliver finds rational horses and filthy human animals, and spends the voyage explaining England to a master who has no word for falsehood. The account convinces him: he learns to speak in whinnies, is expelled by an assembly that cannot see why a Yahoo should be kept, and comes home unable to be in a room with his family.

scenes.title: Arrival
scenes.summary: Mutiny, the shore, the Yahoos, and the slow acquisition of a language with no term for saying the thing which is not.

scenes.title: England described
scenes.summary: War, law, money, medicine and ministers, set out plainly and heard by someone with no reason to make allowances.

scenes.title: A happy life
scenes.summary: Houyhnhnm virtue, education and marriage; Gulliver keeps house, imitates their gait and voice, and calls these the happiest years of his life.

scenes.title: Expulsion and return
scenes.summary: The assembly exhorts his master to send him away; Don Pedro’s kindness is unbearable, and Gulliver ends among horses in his own stable.

characters.name: Lemuel Gulliver
characters.role: Ship’s surgeon, then captain, and the book’s narrator
characters.summary: A competent, incurious man who measures everything and understands almost nothing, and whose plainness makes the satire work. He is not a fixed point the reader can stand on: each voyage adjusts what he admires, and by the fourth he faints when his wife kisses him.
characters.clue: He records latitudes, cargoes and the exact height of everything he meets, learns each new language quickly, and comes home at last preferring the conversation of his horses.

characters.name: The Emperor of Lilliput
characters.role: Sovereign of a country six inches high
characters.summary: Taller than his courtiers by the breadth of a fingernail, and described in the vocabulary of universal monarchy. He is generous while Gulliver is useful and merciful in the technical sense afterwards: the sentence of blinding is presented at court as an act of clemency.
characters.clue: He is almost the breadth of a nail taller than any of his court, describes himself as the delight and terror of the universe, and calls it mercy when he only orders your eyes put out.

characters.name: The King of Brobdingnag
characters.role: A ruler who asks questions and waits for the answers
characters.summary: Swift’s one straightforwardly admirable figure, and a deliberately limited one: he is learned, he keeps a small army, and he cannot conceive of a state secret worth a massacre. His verdict on English history is delivered after several audiences of careful notes, and so it is hard to dismiss.
characters.clue: He questions his six-inch guest about England over several sittings, takes notes, and concludes that the natives of that island are the most pernicious little vermin nature ever suffered to crawl.

characters.name: Glumdalclitch
characters.role: The farmer’s daughter, nine years old and forty feet tall
characters.summary: She names him, sews his shirts, teaches him the language and is the only person in four voyages who loves him. Swift lets her stand outside the satire entirely, and when an eagle carries his box out to sea, Gulliver’s first thought is of her grief.
characters.clue: Nine years old and not above forty feet high, being little for her age, she lines a travelling box with her doll’s quilt and gives its occupant a name meaning mannikin.

characters.name: Lord Munodi
characters.role: A nobleman of Balnibarbi with a working estate
characters.summary: His fields are full, his house stands up and his neighbours despise him for it, because his methods are the old ones. Munodi keeps the Academy funny as well as grotesque: the country has failed because ingenuity has been put in charge of farming, and it never lacked ingenuity.
characters.clue: Once governor of the capital, he is the one lord whose land is well farmed, and he let the projectors talk him into pulling down a good mill to build a new one up a mountain.

characters.name: The Struldbrugs
characters.summary: Born with a spot over the eyebrow, they never die and they also never stop ageing. Swift uses them to separate two wishes that are usually confused, and the chapter’s real cruelty is that Gulliver delivers his rapturous plan for an immortal life before he is taken to see any of them.
characters.clue: A red circular spot over the left eyebrow marks them at birth; at eighty they are declared legally dead, and they go on for centuries after that.

characters.name: Gulliver’s Houyhnhnm master
characters.role: The horse who teaches him the language and hears his account of England
characters.summary: Patient, literal and entirely without a concept of deception, he can only call a lie “the thing which was not”, and Gulliver has to explain a lawsuit to him from first principles. His difficulty in believing the account is the engine of Part IV: everything sounds worse when explained to someone who cannot supply the usual excuses.
characters.clue: He has no word for lying and must be taught one before his guest can describe a European law court.

characters.name: The Yahoos
characters.summary: Filthy, greedy, tribal and recognisably human, they are the satire’s hardest device because Gulliver accepts the identification completely and the book does not obviously stop him. They hoard coloured stones they cannot use, which is the one detail that makes the resemblance impossible to argue with.
characters.clue: Kept in a kennel by their masters and harnessed to sledges, they will dig with their claws for whole days to get at a shining stone.

characters.name: Don Pedro de Mendez
characters.role: The Portuguese captain who takes Gulliver home
characters.summary: He has a raving man brought aboard for his own safety, clothes him, takes him into his own house at Lisbon and asks nothing in return, and Gulliver can barely stand to breathe near him. Swift plants an entirely good human being in the last chapters, and lets his narrator fail to notice, which is the strongest evidence that Swift does not share Gulliver’s final opinion of mankind.
characters.clue: A Portuguese captain who takes a raving stranger into his own house in Lisbon, has a suit of clothes made for him, and lends him twenty pounds for the voyage home.

themes.name: Scale and perspective
themes.summary: Size is an argument here. At twelve to one Gulliver finds Lilliputian politics comic; at one to twelve he finds Brobdingnagian skin disgusting and hears the king condemn English politics. The same facts about Europe are funny in Part I and monstrous in Part II, and only the vantage point has moved.
themes.development: Giant, then miniature, then a tourist at the ordinary human scale in Part III, and finally an animal being classified by someone else in Part IV.

themes.name: Pride
themes.summary: The book ends on pride: in his last paragraph Gulliver can put up with a lawyer, a pickpocket or a politician, but not a Yahoo smitten with pride. The target is the claim to be a reasoning creature, and the Houyhnhnm master offers a humbler description: animals to whose share some small pittance of reason has fallen.
themes.development: National pride in Part I, personal vanity in Part II, intellectual pride in Part III, and species pride in Part IV, where Gulliver catches it himself in the act of despising Yahoos.

themes.name: Reason and its uses
themes.summary: The Laputans calculate beautifully and cannot build a house that stands; the Academy improves agriculture into famine; the perfectly rational Houyhnhnms debate in their general assembly whether to exterminate the Yahoos. Reason cut off from use, and reason cut off from mercy, are both examined, and neither is spared.
themes.development: Munodi’s working farm sets the standard in Part III; the general assembly in Part IV shows what the standard costs when applied without feeling.

themes.name: Party, office and faction
themes.summary: High heels and low, big ends and little: Swift reduces confessional and party conflict to distinctions with no content and then counts the dead. Office in Lilliput goes to the best rope-dancer, and the coloured silks to whoever leaps over or creeps under the emperor’s stick most nimbly: a joke about preferment that explains a good deal of it.
themes.development: Local and topical in Part I, generalised into a European history of war in Part II, and restated to a creature with no politics at all in Part IV, Chapter V.

themes.name: Travel, discovery and possession
themes.summary: Gulliver measures, classifies and reports every people he meets, which is exactly what the voyage literature of the period did. The last chapter turns the habit inside out by explaining how a new country is normally taken, and then exempting his own discoveries on the grounds that they are not worth the trouble.
themes.development: The Lilliputian inventory of his pockets in Part I is the first survey; his refusal to help enslave Blefuscu is the first refusal; Part IV, Chapter XII states the case plainly.

themes.name: Bodies and disgust
themes.summary: Swift will not let the reader forget that a human being is a body that eats, sweats and smells. Gulliver’s excretions are a practical problem in Lilliput, the giant nurses are unbearable at close range, and home from Part IV he finds the very smell of his wife and children intolerable and talks to his horses four hours a day.
themes.development: Comic in Part I, magnified and clinical in Part II, and finally moralised in Part IV, where disgust at the body becomes disgust at the species.

techniques.name: Mock travel writing
techniques.definition: Borrowing the apparatus of factual voyage literature (dates, bearings, cargoes, vocabularies) for an invented country.
techniques.inThisBook: Each voyage opens with a ship, a date and a latitude, and the first edition carried maps; the fiction is guaranteed by exactly the machinery that guaranteed Dampier.

techniques.name: Deadpan narration
techniques.definition: Reporting the outrageous in the tone reserved for the ordinary, leaving the reader to supply the judgement.
techniques.inThisBook: Gulliver blames his own want of courtly training for failing to see the lenity of a sentence of blinding, and puts the King of Brobdingnag’s horror at gunpowder down to a nice, unnecessary scruple. Both times the flat voice leaves the reader to supply the judgement.

techniques.name: Defamiliarisation
techniques.definition: Describing a known thing from outside, in terms that do not name it.
techniques.inThisBook: A pocket watch becomes an engine that makes a noise like a water-mill and is filed as a possible god; the law becomes a society bred up to prove that white is black, and a lie becomes the thing which was not.

techniques.name: Satirical escalation
techniques.definition: Arranging a sequence so that each part is harder to laugh off than the last.
techniques.inThisBook: Rope-dancers, then gunpowder, then the Academy, then a reasoned proposal to exterminate a species: the structure is a slope.

techniques.name: Mock documents
techniques.definition: Prefaces, letters and publisher’s notes that stand outside the narrative and vouch for it.
techniques.inThisBook: Sympson certifies Gulliver’s truthfulness, and Gulliver then attacks Sympson for corrupting the text, so the guarantee and the complaint cancel each other before Chapter I.

techniques.name: Exact measurement
techniques.definition: Precise numbers used where a vague impression would do.
techniques.inThisBook: Six inches, a twelfth, 1,728 Lilliputian meals, the compass of a silver threepence: the arithmetic is kept up with care, and it makes the impossible countries feel surveyed.

quotations.text: I do, in the next place, complain of my own great want of judgment, in being prevailed upon by the entreaties and false reasoning of you and some others, very much against my own opinion, to suffer my travels to be published.
quotations.reference: A Letter from Captain Gulliver to His Cousin Sympson
quotations.context: The prefatory letter added for Faulkner’s edition, written years after the voyages.
quotations.analysis: The book opens by regretting its own publication. Swift builds a paratext that quarrels with itself, with a publisher vouching for the text and an author disowning it, so that a reader who wants to know what is authoritative here has nowhere to stand before the first voyage begins.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, A Letter from Captain Gulliver to His Cousin Sympson

quotations.text: they shouted for joy, and danced upon my breast, repeating several times as they did at first, “Hekinah degul.”
quotations.context: After Gulliver has drunk two hogsheads of Lilliputian wine while pegged to the ground.
quotations.analysis: The foreign words are left untranslated, so the reader is put exactly where Gulliver is: watching a ceremony and guessing at its meaning. Swift also gets the scale into the verb (they dance on his chest), which makes the wonder physical before it is political.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter I

quotations.text: we conjecture it is either some unknown animal, or the god that he worships; but we are more inclined to the latter opinion
quotations.context: From the official inventory two Lilliputian officers make of Gulliver’s pockets.
quotations.analysis: The officers reason correctly from what they can observe: the object is consulted before every action, so it governs him. Swift’s joke about a nation that worships the clock is delivered entirely inside a customs document, and the form of the passage, a numbered search of a man’s body, is as pointed as its content.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter II

quotations.text: It is allowed on all hands, that the primitive way of breaking eggs, before we eat them, was upon the larger end
quotations.context: Reldresal explaining the origin of the war with Blefuscu.
quotations.analysis: The phrase ‘allowed on all hands’ is the vocabulary of settled doctrine applied to breakfast. Swift then supplies casualty figures, eleven thousand who chose death over submission, so the cause stays trivial while the consequences are at full historical size.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter IV

quotations.text: his majesty has determined to make use only of low heels in the administration of the government
quotations.context: The same conversation, on the two parties of the empire.
quotations.analysis: Party is reduced to footwear and the reduction changes nothing about how the politics behaves: patronage follows the heel height, and the heir hedges by wearing one of each and walking with a hobble. The satire is that a small difference is enough.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter IV

quotations.text: They look upon fraud as a greater crime than theft, and therefore seldom fail to punish it with death
quotations.context: Gulliver’s account of Lilliputian laws, which he reports with approval.
quotations.analysis: This chapter is the one place where Lilliput is used as a model, and the reasoning is commercial: honesty has no defence against fraud, so credit collapses without it. Swift puts his own convictions into the mouth of a ridiculous state, which stops the book being read as simple contempt.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter VI

quotations.text: I cannot but conclude the bulk of your natives to be the most pernicious race of little odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon the surface of the earth.”
quotations.context: The king’s conclusion after several audiences on the history and constitution of England.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built to sound judicial: he has recapitulated, compared question with answer, and only then delivers. The king is stroking Gulliver as he gives the verdict, so contempt and gentleness arrive in the same gesture.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part II, Chapter VI

quotations.text: The king was struck with horror at the description I had given of those terrible engines, and the proposal I had made.
quotations.context: After Gulliver has offered the king the secret of gunpowder as a proof of his usefulness.
quotations.analysis: The reversal is complete and Gulliver misses it entirely: he files the refusal under the king’s narrow principles and nice scruples. Swift lets the reader hold two readings of the same scene, and the satire lives in the gap between them.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part II, Chapter VII

quotations.text: whoever could make two ears of corn, or two blades of grass, to grow upon a spot of ground where only one grew before, would deserve better of mankind, and do more essential service to his country, than the whole race of politicians put together.”
quotations.context: Gulliver reporting the king’s opinion of what constitutes useful knowledge.
quotations.analysis: The standard offered here is the one the whole book measures learning against, and it is agricultural: does it feed anybody? Part III is built to fail this test, which is why the Academy of Lagado comes a hundred pages after this sentence.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part II, Chapter VII

quotations.text: he proceeds to the last remedy, by letting the island drop directly upon their heads, which makes a universal destruction both of houses and men.
quotations.context: The means by which the king of Laputa suppresses a rebellious town below.
quotations.analysis: The flying island is a machine for occupation: it blocks the sun and rain first, and only crushes as a last resort. Swift gives the tactic a bureaucratic sequence of escalating measures, and the chapter then explains why the king hesitates: his own estates are down there, and the island’s bottom might crack.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter III

quotations.text: He has been eight years upon a project for extracting sunbeams out of cucumbers, which were to be put in phials hermetically sealed, and let out to warm the air in raw inclement summers.
quotations.context: The first projector Gulliver meets in the grand academy of Lagado.
quotations.analysis: In principle the project is a reasonable one, a scheme to store summer heat, which is why it is dangerous: the man is eight years in and asking for funds. Swift attacks the institution that pays for eight years of curiosity while the country outside has stopped growing food.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter V

quotations.text: Perjury, oppression, subornation, fraud, pandarism, and the like infirmities, were among the most excusable arts they had to mention; and for these I gave, as it was reasonable, great allowance.
quotations.context: In Glubbdubdrib, where the governor can summon the dead and question them.
quotations.analysis: The list is arranged as a descent and then stopped short, so the reader waits for what could possibly be worse. Swift’s device here is a historian’s: the dead are called up to correct the record that the living have written about them.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter VIII

quotations.text: “Happy nation, where every child hath at least a chance for being immortal! Happy people, who enjoy so many living examples of ancient virtue, and have masters ready to instruct them in the wisdom of all former ages!
quotations.context: Gulliver’s reaction on first hearing that some Luggnaggians never die, before he has met one.
quotations.analysis: Swift makes him deliver the whole eloquent programme (wealth, learning, a record of the ages) and only then takes him to see the Struldbrugs. The chapter separates two things the wish for immortality usually keeps welded together, and Gulliver has already committed himself in public before the distinction arrives.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter X

quotations.text: They were the most mortifying sight I ever beheld; and the women more horrible than the men.
quotations.context: Meeting five or six Struldbrugs of various ages at Luggnagg.
quotations.analysis: The correction is flat and brief after the rapture, and the second clause, that the women are worse, is the period’s ordinary misogyny surfacing in a passage about the horror of not dying. Swift’s satire and Swift’s prejudices are in the same sentence, and an honest reading has to hold both.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter X

quotations.text: “that the use of speech was to make us understand one another, and to receive information of facts; now, if anyone said the thing which was not, these ends were defeated, because I cannot properly be said to understand him
quotations.context: The Houyhnhnm master working out what Gulliver can mean by a lie.
quotations.analysis: The argument is a definition: if speech exists to convey facts, a false sentence is void, and leaves the hearer worse informed than silence would. It takes the master some difficulty to grasp the concept at all, and Gulliver needs it before he can explain a single English institution.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter IV

quotations.text: in recounting the numbers of those who have been killed in battle, I cannot but think you have said the thing which is not.”
quotations.context: The master’s response to Gulliver’s account of European wars and their casualties.
quotations.analysis: The Houyhnhnm phrase for lying is used, for once, against Gulliver, and it is used because the truth is too large to be credible. Swift gets the sharpest effect available to satire here: the honest report of Europe is indistinguishable, to a reasonable listener, from an invention.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter V

quotations.text: I enjoyed perfect health of body, and tranquillity of mind; I did not feel the treachery or inconstancy of a friend, nor the injuries of a secret or open enemy.
quotations.context: Gulliver’s account of his settled life among the Houyhnhnms.
quotations.analysis: The happiness is described entirely by subtraction (no treachery, no enemy, no bribes, no informers), so the paragraph is a catalogue of England with the sign reversed. He is at his most contented exactly where he has nobody of his own kind to be content with.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter X

quotations.text: wherein I have not been so studious of ornament as of truth.
quotations.context: The opening of the last chapter, addressed to the reader.
quotations.analysis: The claim to plainness is the oldest guarantee in travel writing and Swift has spent four voyages making it worthless. Gulliver closes the account with the same promise Sympson opened it with, and by now the reader has seen what his plain reporting can be made to carry.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter XII

quotations.text: principal design was to inform, and not to amuse thee.
quotations.context: The same paragraph, on his purpose in publishing.
quotations.analysis: Six words that the nursery versions of the book leave out. Set beside the letter to Sympson, where Gulliver complains that nobody has reformed in six months, the sentence is already an admission of failure.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter XII

quotations.text: when I behold a lump of deformity and diseases, both in body and mind, smitten with pride, it immediately breaks all the measures of my patience
quotations.context: The final paragraph of the book, on what he can and cannot tolerate in his own species.
quotations.analysis: He will forgive humanity its natural vices and not its pride, which is the very vice he is displaying while he says so, and Swift has him admit as much a few lines earlier. The book ends by catching its narrator in the fault the book exists to attack.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter XII

timeline.label: Jonathan Swift born in Dublin
timeline.detail: Educated at Kilkenny and Trinity College, Dublin, and later secretary to Sir William Temple.

timeline.label: The book’s date for Gulliver’s first voyage: 4 May 1699
timeline.detail: The fictional first voyage is dated 4 May 1699; the book dates every departure.

timeline.label: A Tale of a Tub and The Battle of the Books published
timeline.detail: Swift’s first sustained attack on false learning and modern authorship, and an anonymous one.

timeline.label: Swift installed as Dean of St Patrick’s, Dublin
timeline.detail: The post he held for the rest of his life, and the source of the name by which Ireland knew him.

timeline.label: Swift writes The Drapier’s Letters
timeline.detail: Swift’s campaign against Wood’s halfpence, written in the voice of a Dublin draper: another invented plain-speaking narrator.

timeline.label: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World published
timeline.detail: Benjamin Motte issues it in two volumes on 28 October, with Lemuel Gulliver on the title page.

timeline.label: Keys, sequels and imitations appear
timeline.detail: Explanatory ‘keys’, spurious continuations and parodies follow within months of publication.

timeline.label: Swift’s A Modest Proposal published
timeline.detail: The same deadpan applied to Irish famine, by a narrator whose arithmetic is as careful as Gulliver’s.

timeline.label: Faulkner’s Dublin edition
timeline.detail: The Travels appear in volume III of Swift’s collected works, with the letter to Sympson added.

timeline.label: Swift dies in Dublin
timeline.detail: He left the bulk of his estate to found a hospital for the mentally ill.

timeline.label: Fleischer Studios’ animated Gulliver’s Travels
timeline.detail: One of the best-known screen versions, and a clear case of the book surviving as Lilliput alone.

timeline.label: Television adaptation of all four voyages
timeline.detail: Unusually among adaptations, it keeps Part IV and Gulliver’s damaged return.

places.name: Nottinghamshire
places.note: Gulliver’s father’s small estate, and the county he retires to at the end.

places.name: Emanuel College, Cambridge
places.note: Where Gulliver was sent at fourteen before being apprenticed to a London surgeon.

places.name: Leyden
places.note: Where he studied physic for two years and seven months, the standard training for a ship’s surgeon.

places.name: Bristol
places.note: The port from which the Antelope sails for the South Sea in 1699.

places.name: Nangasac
places.note: Nagasaki, the one real country Gulliver visits, reached from Luggnagg in Part III.

places.name: Amsterdam
places.note: His route home from Japan, and the port whose Dutch traders he treats with a marked and pointed hostility.

criticalViews.work: The English Humourists of the Eighteenth Century
criticalViews.summary: In a lecture of 1851 Thackeray condemned the fourth voyage as horrible, shameful and blasphemous, filthy in thought, furious and obscene. He later softened his view of Swift.

criticalViews.essay: Politics vs. Literature: An Examination of Gulliver’s Travels
criticalViews.summary: Orwell called Swift a Tory anarchist whose disgust with the human body poisons the last voyage, and saw in the Houyhnhnms a totalitarian society that rules by unanimous opinion. He still counted it among the six books he would save if all others were destroyed.
